title: Borrow Mat
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the subtraction chapter. An adult sees a column sum being filled in, which a child could do on squared paper. What is actually being settled is the direction of a trade. When a column cannot pay, the ten is fetched from the column on its left and that column is left one less, and a child who reaches the other way, or who enlarges the digit and never reduces anything, gets a wrong answer by a method that looks perfectly right on the line.

writeup.why: Take one long number off another on a column mat, and find out where the ten comes from when a column has not got enough to give.
writeup.look: A ruled mat with a heading over every column, the greater number above the smaller one with a rule between them, and a tray of bundles beside it.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Borrow Mat' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns settled against the columns the mat is ruled for, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column closes and the second fixed at the width of the mat, with the count of columns that have had to fetch a ten standing beside them. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The mat sits across the top of the working area, 800 by 370 at 207,202. Along its top runs a trade band 68 tall, empty until a trade is made and never scrolled; under that, headings 44 tall; under those, the minuend row and the subtrahend row, each of cells 84 tall, with the minus sign standing 40 to the left of the lower row; then a rule 6 tall running the full width of the mat; then the difference row 84 tall beneath it. The columns are ruled 128 wide under their headings and drawn from the right, so the ones column is always the rightmost and a five column mat is this same mat with its leftmost column left unruled. A number arrives as a strip of digit cards drawn joined into one piece, each card 96 by 76 sitting centred in its column, so a strip slides as a whole and no single digit can be pulled out of it. A strip may be dropped anywhere along the mat, including where its right end hangs over open columns, and the heading standing over each of its digits is read out afresh as it moves. A column that is tapped lights the full height of both upper rows and writes its answer in green under the rule; with the ones first control locked, only the rightmost unsettled column will light at all, and a column tapped out of turn names the column that has to settle before it and gives nothing else away. Where the digit above is smaller than the digit below, the column refuses to close and its two digits are held lit. A reach made to the column on the LEFT strikes that column's digit through once with a single stroke, writes its new and smaller value in rose small above it in the trade band, and draws the ten arriving in the trade band over the column that could not pay, in vermilion, with a short arrow running from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right and never the other way. A reach made to the right instead springs back with nothing marked, the proper lending column on the left lights, and the arrow is redrawn the right way round. The bundle tray runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 112 at 64,598, holding bundles of ten drawn as ten countable things under one visible tie and loose things beside them; untying a bundle for a column lays out exactly ten separate things and leaves the empty tie lying where the bundle stood. Replay trades dims every column that paid on its own and walks the finished working again showing only the columns that traded, in the order they traded in. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a column answer or a whole difference is asked for, and on the first phase a word pad of the mat's own words, ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, minuend, subtrahend and difference, so that a row can be named and a column called with one press. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the greater number standing on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, the answer under the rule is green, the ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, and a zero that is only holding a place open is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every one of the readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a column that has lent is told by the single strike through its digit and by the smaller value written small above it. A struck lending digit is never rubbed out and never redrawn whole: the stroke through it and the smaller value above it stay on the mat until the working is cleared, because that pair is the half of the trade that actually cost something.
writeup.finish: The card shows the longest working the child built, its columns still named, every struck lending digit still showing and the tally of trades beside it.

phases.win: all three labels land on the right rows and the working is read aloud
phases.does: labels the row on top, the row under it and the answer, then reads it out
phases.goal: the three rows of a written subtraction can be named
phases.says: Point at the number on top. Now the one under it. Now the answer. Name each one.
phases.check: Away from the screen: write a subtraction of your own on squared paper, then point at its minuend, its subtrahend and its difference in that order.
phases.feels: three rows, three names, and the names belong to the rows rather than to the numbers standing in them
phases.hands: On squared paper write the column headings first, one to a square, then a five digit number with a smaller one under it, one digit to a square, and rule a line under the lower number. Before a single column is worked, write the three names down the left of the page against the rows they belong to. Then ask which of the three names is the only one that is not yet a number on the page.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which of these rows was on the page before any working was done? Second rung, the phase's: which row did the working make? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns with a finished subtraction on it and the child lays the three plates on those three rows. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the number taken away and the answer both sit below the number on top, and the bottom row looks like the one that gets the last of the three names.
wrong.move: calls the answer under the rule the subtrahend, because it is the lowest row on the mat.
wrong.screen: the rule is drawn heavier and the two rows above it lift a little together while each is read out as a number that was there before any working started; the row below the rule stays down and is read out as what the working made. The child's plate stays exactly where it was put, so the two readings can be held against each other, and nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: three names and three rows look as though they ought to pair off in whatever order each was met, and the list was read downwards while the eye was travelling up.
wrong.move: lays the three plates on the rows in the order the three words were heard, working from the bottom row upwards.
wrong.screen: the working is read aloud row by row from the top, the row being read lighting as it goes, and every plate stays exactly where the child put it; where a plate names a row that the reading does not match, that plate and that row are ringed in amber and stay ringed. No plate is ever moved for the child.

phases.screen: a finished subtraction on the mat with the naming control waiting
phases.soWhat: The number on top is the minuend, the number taken away is the subtrahend, and the answer under the rule is the difference.
phases.concept: Three names for the three numbers

phases.win: the greater strip settles on the upper row and the swapped attempt runs out of things to take
phases.does: chooses which strip goes on top, then tries it the other way round
phases.goal: the greater number goes on top and the two cannot be swapped
phases.says: Which one goes on top? Try it the other way and say what goes wrong.
phases.check: Adding lets you write its two numbers in either order. Say what happens when you try that in a subtraction.
phases.feels: swapping the two numbers over does not give a different answer, it gives no answer at all
phases.hands: Write 26,153 above 71,408 on squared paper, that way round, and try to work the ones column out loud. Then write the same two numbers the other way up, work them, and check the answer by adding it back on to 26,153. Ask what the first arrangement was actually asking for.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which of the two numbers has more in it? Second rung, the phase's: can you take more away from a number than the number holds? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns with two small strips on the ledge and the child chooses which one goes up. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: two numbers being added may be written in either order and the total does not change, and nothing about a written subtraction announces that the rule has stopped applying.
wrong.move: puts the strip that was read out first on top, because the chapter before this one let two numbers be swapped over.
wrong.screen: the pair is worked on the mat exactly as the child laid it, from the ones leftwards, and the first column with less above than below is held lit with both digits showing and the reach refused because the column on its left has nothing left to lend either. The same pair is then laid the other way up on a second mat below the first, worked through to 45,255, and both mats are left standing together.

wrong.why: a column turned round quietly gives an answer where there was not one, and a page of columns that all worked looks like a page that went well.
wrong.move: keeps the smaller number on top and takes the smaller digit from the greater one in each column, so that every column pays.
wrong.screen: each column is read out in the order it is written, the upper digit named first and the lower one second, and every column the child turned round is ringed amber and read again as it stands. The answer the child built stays under the rule, the same pair is worked the right way up beside it, and the check by addition is run on both: only one of the two totals lands back on the number the working started from.

phases.screen: two loose number strips beside an empty mat with two rows waiting
phases.soWhat: The greater number goes on top and the smaller one under it, and that is not a choice you get to make.
phases.concept: The smaller number comes off the greater one

phases.win: the lending column is struck and rewritten one less, and the ten arrives on its right
phases.does: reaches to the column on the left, strikes its digit down by one and takes the ten
phases.goal: a ten is fetched from the column on the left, which is left one less
phases.says: This column cannot pay. Which way do you reach for a ten?
phases.check: Away from the screen: work 85,402 - 31,271 on squared paper. Which column has to lend, and what is that column left standing at?
phases.feels: the column that lends is left standing one less, and the ten that arrives is exactly what that column gave up
phases.hands: Give the child bundles of ten straws and a few loose ones, and ask for an amount to be taken away whose ones digit is bigger than the loose pile allows. Let them untie a bundle themselves. Then, on squared paper, work 42,376 - 18,159 and insist on the answer being said in two halves every time a column cannot pay: the ten arrives here, and the column on the left is left one less. Ask how many bundles are standing at the end and why that count dropped when nothing was taken out of the bundles themselves.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which column is worth ten of the column that cannot pay? Second rung, the phase's: after a column has lent, is there more in it or less? Third rung: the mat is cut to two columns with one trade in it and the bundle tray opens itself, and the child unties the bundle before the reach is made. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the hand has just come from the right, the column there is settled and quiet, and nothing written on the line says which way a ten travels.
wrong.move: reaches to the column on the RIGHT for the ten, because that is the column just finished and it looks like the one with something to spare.
wrong.screen: the drag springs back with nothing marked and nothing cleared. The column on the LEFT lights instead, the arrow is drawn again running from it to the column that could not pay, and the two columns are read out by what each is worth, so that the column on the left is heard to be worth ten of the column beside it and the column on the right is heard to be worth a tenth of it. The refused reach stays drawn as a faint line so that the two directions can be seen at once.

wrong.why: the column can be made to pay simply by writing more in it, and with nothing struck anywhere on the line the working reads perfectly well from top to bottom.
wrong.move: writes a bigger digit over the one above and takes the lower digit from that, leaving every other column standing exactly as it was.
wrong.screen: the enlarged digit the child wrote stays exactly where it is. The whole upper row is then counted out in the bundle tray, bundles and loose things together, and it comes to more than the number the working began with, with the extra ten lit in the tray. The lending column is left untouched and unstruck throughout, so what is showing is a ten with nowhere to have come from.

phases.screen: a ones column whose upper digit is smaller than the one below it
phases.soWhat: When a column cannot pay, fetch the ten from the column on its left and strike that column's digit down by one.
phases.concept: A column that cannot pay borrows from its left

phases.win: the last column on the left settles, the tally stops and no new rule was needed
phases.does: settles the ones and moves left one column at a time to the end
phases.goal: a long subtraction is the same work with more columns
phases.says: Start at the ones and go left. Say each column as you finish it.
phases.check: How many column steps does a subtraction of two six digit numbers take, and which of those steps has to be done first?
phases.feels: six columns, three of them trading and three paying on their own, and not one new thing to learn
phases.hands: Take a four digit subtraction the child has already worked on paper and write two more digits in front of each number to make them six digits long. Work 9,18,473 - 3,25,916 on squared paper and put a tick above every column that had to fetch a ten. Then count the ticks and ask whether any one of those steps was a kind of step they had not done before.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many columns is the mat ruled for? Second rung, the phase's: how many of them have an answer under the rule yet? Third rung: the mat is cut back to four columns, the child works it through, and then two columns are opened at the left and the same working is done again. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: reading and writing both run from the left, and the leftmost column is where the number looks as though it begins.
wrong.move: works the leftmost column first and travels rightwards, the way a number is read out.
wrong.screen: every answer the child wrote stays under the rule exactly where it was put. The ones first control then locks itself, the same pair is worked again from the right with one column lighting at a time, and the two runs stand one under the other with the order of work numbered beside each column; the columns where a later trade changed a digit that had already been used are ringed amber in the first run and stay ringed.

wrong.why: two or three columns in a row have just had to fetch, and a run like that looks like a rule about the whole number rather than about each column on its own.
wrong.move: fetches a ten in every column after the first one that needed it, as though a trade once begun had to carry on to the end.
wrong.screen: the columns are opened again one at a time from the right with both of their digits lit, and each column that can pay on its own closes with the trade band above it left completely empty while the trade count holds still. The trades the child wrote where nothing was needed stay drawn where they are, and the difference the mat builds stands under the one the child built so the two can be read against each other column by column.

phases.screen: the mat grown to six columns with two six digit strips on it
phases.soWhat: A longer subtraction is the same method with more steps, and it still starts at the ones column.
phases.concept: Work from the ones and go leftwards

writeup.delight: The third phase, at the moment the reach lands. The two halves of the trade are drawn as one movement rather than two: the stroke goes through the lending digit and the smaller value appears above it at the very instant the ten lands in the trade band over the column that could not pay, joined by the little arrow running left to right. Drag the ten back out of the receiving column and the whole thing runs backwards, the stroke lifting off the lending digit and the digit standing whole again, so the trade can be made and unmade as often as a finger likes. Nothing else on the mat moves while it happens and the voice says nothing at all.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a finished subtraction stands on the mat with its difference already under the rule and three naming plates lying unplaced on the ledge. On the second the mat stands empty with two rows ruled and waiting, and two loose digit strips lie side by side on the ledge below it, neither of them on the mat at all. On the third a five column mat holds two strips home in their columns with the ones column lit, its upper digit smaller than the digit under it, and every other column still closed. On the fourth the mat stands six columns wide with a six digit strip on each of its two rows and the answer row empty from end to end. The running count at the top left holds the columns settled against the columns the mat is ruled for, with the trade count beside them, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first naming plate, or the greater of the two loose strips, or the lit ones column, or the rightmost column of the six, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks for the two numbers to be read as they stand. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two numbers up to six digits, with the bundle tray, the naming labels and the trade tally switched on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming the three parts, putting the greater number on top, fetching a ten from the column on the left, and working five and six digit numbers from the ones.
voiceLines: A ruled mat, and two numbers lined up by their right ends. The greater one on top.
Point at the number on top. Now the one under it. Now the answer. Name each one.
Which one goes on top? Try it the other way and say what goes wrong.
This column cannot pay. Which way do you reach for a ten?
Start at the ones and go left. Say each column as you finish it.
Another pair. The ones column first, then leftwards to the end.
Free play. Any two numbers, with the bundle tray, the naming labels and the tally as you like.
Reach the other way. A ten only ever comes out of the column on the left.
Every column settled, and every column that lent is standing one less than it was.

observations.why: The ten that arrived came out of that column, so that column has less in it than it had.
observations.soWhat: A trade has two halves, and the half that costs is the one on the left.
observations.observe: The column that lent kept its digit, struck through once, with a smaller value written above it.

observations.why: The column on the left is worth ten of the column beside it, so it is the only column with a ten to give.
observations.soWhat: The direction of the reach is fixed by what the columns are worth, not by which hand is free.
observations.observe: The ten always arrived from the same side, on a five column mat and on a six column one alike.

observations.why: A trade made on the right changes a digit on the left, so a column worked early can be undone by one made later.
observations.soWhat: The ones column goes first and the work runs leftwards, and that order is part of the method.
observations.observe: The mat would not open a column until the column on its right had settled.

observations.why: Every column is worked the same way whatever its heading says, and a longer number is only more of them.
observations.soWhat: A six digit subtraction is a five digit one with another column on the end.
observations.observe: Growing the mat from five columns to six added steps and no new rule at all.

source_tool.description: A ruled mat fills the stage with one column for each place and a named heading over every column. Two numbers arrive as strips of digit cards and settle with their right ends aligned, the greater one above and the smaller one below it with a minus sign to its left, and a rule is drawn between the lower strip and the empty answer row. A naming control labels the three rows as the minuend, the subtrahend and the difference. The columns are worked one at a time from the ones leftwards, and the mat will not let a column be worked before the column on its right is settled. Where the digit above is smaller than the digit below, the column will not close: the child reaches to the column on its LEFT, that lending digit is struck through once and its new and smaller value is written small above it, and the ten it lent is drawn arriving here, so the taking and the giving are one movement rather than two. A reach taken to the right instead is handed back with the proper lending column lit and the arrow redrawn the right way round. A bundle tray beside the mat unties a bundle of ten into ten loose things for any column that asks for it, so the trade can be counted rather than believed. A trade tally along the top counts how many columns had to fetch a ten.
source_tool.art_direction: Two digit strips on a ruled column mat / Picture book

audio.note: Web Audio oscillators, no files. The same three cues in every tool of every Class 4 chapter, so the grade sounds like one grade.

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, bundles of ten that untie themselves, a rule between the number taken away and the answer, and a number line strip for the rounding work.

A subtraction is always shown with its columns visible: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the greater number on top, the two numbers aligned by their right ends, the minus sign to the left of the lower row, and a horizontal rule between that row and the answer. A bare line of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach taking away.

A trade is always drawn as both of its halves. The lending column keeps its digit, struck through once, with its new and smaller value written small above it, and the ten it lent is drawn arriving in the column on its right. A short arrow runs from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right, never the other way.

A check by addition is drawn under the subtraction it tests, and the total it comes to is set beside the number the working started from, so the two can be read against each other without anything being cleared.
Where tokens or bundles stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn and they stay countable at a glance and never overlap.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The greater number on top is deep blue, the number being taken away is amber, and the answer under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The ten lifted out of the column on the left is vermilion, and a digit rewritten after the trade has been made is rose, so the two halves of one trade are told apart at a glance. A zero holding a place open is grey, because it is a placeholder and not a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a lending column is told apart by the strike through its digit and by the smaller digit written above it before it is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Reach the other way. A ten only ever comes out of the column on the left.
voice.onNext: Another pair. The ones column first, then leftwards to the end.
voice.opening: A ruled mat, and two numbers lined up by their right ends. The greater one on top.
voice.onFinish: Every column settled, and every column that lent is standing one less than it was.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any two numbers, with the bundle tray, the naming labels and the tally as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: Straight after the first subtraction has been set out on squared paper by hand, and before the second one. The tool is what makes the lending column visible at the moment it lends, instead of after the answer has been marked.

answer_key.rule: The greater number goes on top and the smaller one under it, lined up by their right ends so each digit stands in the column of its own place. The greater number is the minuend, the number taken away is the subtrahend, and the answer under the rule is the difference. Work the ones column first and go leftwards. Where the digit above is smaller than the digit below, fetch a ten from the column on its left: that column is left one less than it was, and the ten arrives in the column that could not pay. A five digit or six digit number needs no new rule, only more columns.
answer_key.wrong: The column is opened again and the trade is redrawn slowly: the lending column on the left struck and rewritten one less, then the ten arriving on its right, with the arrow running left to right. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The ones cannot pay, because 5 is smaller than 8, so a ten is fetched from the tens column on its left.
The tens digit drops from 1 to 0 and the ones become 15, so 15 - 8 = 7.
Every column except the leftmost has to fetch a ten in turn, which gives 35,567.
items.answer: 35,567, and the tens column is the first to lend
items.question: Subtract 27,648 from 63,215, and say which column is the first to lend.
items.checkpoint: A ten is fetched from the column on the left, and that column is left one less.
items.misconception: Fetching the ten from the column on the right instead of the column on the left.

steps: Start at the ones: 3 cannot pay 7, so a ten comes from the tens, which drops to 3, and 13 - 7 = 6.
The tens then fetch from the hundreds, and the hundreds pay on their own at 4 - 3 = 1.
The thousands and the ten thousands each fetch a ten in turn, giving 3,72,176 from four trades.
items.answer: 3,72,176, and four columns had to fetch a ten
items.question: Subtract 1,48,367 from 5,20,543, and say how many columns had to fetch a ten.
items.checkpoint: More columns mean more steps, not a new method, and the work still starts at the ones.
items.misconception: Starting at the leftmost column, which hides every trade that is still to come.

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: lays each number on the mat with its right end in the ones column
labels the three rows as the minuend, the subtrahend and the difference
locks the working order so the rightmost column settles first
fetches a ten from the column on the left and strikes that digit down by one
unties a bundle of ten into ten loose things so the trade can be counted
counts how many columns had to fetch a ten in this working
walks the finished working again showing only the trades

teaching_notes: Set the first subtraction out on squared paper by hand before the tool is opened, one digit to a square, with the column headings written in before any digit goes in. Then use the tool for the thing paper cannot do: stop at the first column that cannot pay and ask, before anybody reaches, which way the hand is going to go. Get the answer said in two halves every time, because only one of them costs anything. The ten arrives here, and the column on the left is left one less. A child who says only the first half will enlarge a digit and reduce nothing, and the working will look right the whole way down. Untie a real bundle with the tray for the first few trades, so that ten is a quantity that moved rather than a mark that was written. Keep the ones first control locked until the direction is automatic. The regrouping question about taking eight tens from a three digit number is worth doing on the mat and then with straws: three hundreds, three tens and eight ones become two hundreds, thirteen tens and eight ones, and thirteen tens less eight tens is five tens. Use the naming control on every working and insist on the words, because the finding topic later on cannot be asked for without them.
generation_prompt: Build a column subtraction tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A ruled mat of place value columns, four to six of them, with a named heading over each column. The greater number sits on the upper row and the number being taken away on the row under it, aligned by their right ends, a minus sign to the left of the lower row and a horizontal rule between that row and an empty answer row. A naming control drops labels reading minuend, subtrahend and difference on the three rows. Columns are worked by tapping, in right to left order while the ones first control is locked, and a column tapped out of turn names the column that must settle before it without giving anything else away. When the upper digit of a column is smaller than the lower one, the column refuses to close until a ten is fetched: dragging to the column on the LEFT strikes that column's digit through once, writes its new and smaller value small above it, and animates the ten arriving in the column that could not pay, with a short arrow drawn from the lending column to the receiving one, left to right. A drag to the right instead is refused, the proper lending column is lit and the arrow is redrawn the right way round. A bundle tray beside the mat unties a bundle of ten into ten separate countable things for whichever column asks. A trade tally along the top counts the columns that fetched a ten, and a replay control walks the finished working again showing only the trades. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Put the greater number on top and line the two up by their right ends. Name the three rows before you start. Work the ones column first, then move left. If a column cannot pay, reach to the column on its left and take a ten. Strike that digit down by one before you carry on.
